Claimants can deduct qualifying expenditures and earn investment tax credits of 15% or, for qualifying CCPCs and eligible Canadian public corporations, an enhanced, refundable 35% on up to $6,000,000 of annual qualified expenditures.
Executive Summary and Architectural Overview of the Canadian R&D Tax Regime

Canada maintains one of the most comprehensive and generous fiscal architectures for industrial research and innovation in the developed world, anchored federally by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program. Administered jointly by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) with respect to operational compliance, financial verification, and technical review, and by the Department of Finance Canada with respect to statutory policy and legislative design, the federal SR&ED framework operates through a dual-mechanism structure codified in the Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)) and the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945). In the first statutory stage, subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act permits taxpayers carrying on business in Canada to pool current and—following recent legislative restoration—qualifying capital SR&ED expenditures, deducting those outlays against current-year business income or carrying the undeducted pool balance forward indefinitely to offset taxable income in subsequent taxation years. In the second statutory stage, subsections 127(5) and 127(9) together with section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act grant claimants an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) ranging from a basic rate of 15% to an enhanced rate of 35% on their SR&ED qualified expenditure pool, delivered as a reduction of Part I federal income tax otherwise payable, a direct cash refund, or a combination of both.

The legal and financial contours of the Canadian SR&ED landscape underwent their most significant structural transformation in over a decade with the enactment of Government Bill C-15, An Act to implement certain provisions of the budget tabled in Parliament on November 4, 2025 (short title: Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, Statutes of Canada 2026, Chapter 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Building upon policy consultations initiated in Budget 2024, concrete legislative proposals introduced in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement, and formal measures tabled in Budget 2025, Bill C-15 enacted four foundational expansions retroactive to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (and capital or equipment lease outlays incurred after December 15, 2024). Furthermore, Budget 2026 reinforced this expansionary fiscal trajectory by committing $930 million to broaden the SR&ED program and accelerate the domestic commercialisation of research and development alongside renewed clean technology support through the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP).

Specifically, the statutory amendments enacted under Bill C-15 doubled the annual expenditure limit eligible for the enhanced 35% ITC from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000; expanded the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds governing that expenditure limit from the historical range of $10,000,000 to $50,000,000 to a substantially broader range of $15,000,000 to $75,000,000; extended access to the enhanced 35% refundable ITC beyond Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) to include Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs); and restored the eligibility of depreciable capital property and equipment lease expenditures for both the section 37 deductible expenditure pool and the subsection 127(9) ITC calculation after an eleven-year statutory hiatus that had prevailed between January 1, 2014 and December 15, 2024. Parallel to these statutory reforms, the CRA launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval Process on April 1, 2026, enabling businesses to obtain up-front technical eligibility determinations within eight weeks prior to commencing research work or incurring expenditures, alongside a federal mandate to cut overall claim processing periods in half.

body.text: Beyond the federal regime, virtually every Canadian province and one territory (Yukon) operate complementary R&D tax credit or grant programs that stack atop the federal SR&ED incentive. While most provincial credits—including Ontario's three-tier R&D credit system, British Columbia's 10% SR&ED tax credit (which harmonized directly with Bill C-15 under British Columbia's Bill 2, Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026), Manitoba's 15% R&D credit, Saskatchewan's R&D credit, and the 15% fully refundable credits in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Newfoundland and Labrador—piggyback directly on federal Form T661 technical eligibility and are administered by the CRA, Québec and Alberta maintain autonomous administrative regimes. Revenu Québec independently administers its R&D tax credits (such as the 14% to 30% refundable Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages on Form RD-1029.7-V), whereas Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA) delivers the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) on AT1 Schedule 29, offering an 8% base grant and a 20% incremental grant on R&D spending exceeding a corporation's two-year rolling average. Because provincial R&D credits and direct innovation grants (such as NRC IRAP) are classified as "government assistance" under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18) of the federal Income Tax Act, sophisticated modelling of federal-provincial interaction, assistance grinding, and Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) shielding is essential to maximizing net after-tax recovery.
Statutory and Legislative Foundations of the Federal SR&ED Program
The Architecture of the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations

The legal authority governing federal R&D tax incentives in Canada is bifurcated between primary statutory provisions in the Income Tax Act (ITA) and subordinate regulatory provisions in Part XXIX (sections 2900 to 2903) and Part XI of the Income Tax Regulations (ITR). Unlike jurisdictions that rely on discretionary ministerial decrees or standalone innovation statutes, Canada embeds its R&D incentives directly within the computation of net income for tax purposes (Division B of Part I of the ITA) and the computation of tax payable (Division E of Part I of the ITA).

This structural placement produces a two-stage fiscal benefit. In the first stage, section 37 of the ITA overrides the general capital prohibition in paragraph 18(1)(b) and the ordinary timing rules of section 9 by establishing a dedicated pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures. Expenditures qualifying under subsection 37(1) are aggregated into an expenditure pool at the close of each taxation year. A taxpayer may elect to deduct any portion of the positive balance of this pool in computing net income for the current taxation year, or defer the deduction indefinitely to future taxation years where the corporation generates higher taxable income or faces a higher marginal corporate tax rate. In the second stage, subsection 127(9) of the ITA defines the "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" and "qualified expenditure," which serve as the base for computing the Investment Tax Credit under subsection 127(5) (for non-refundable credits applied against Part I tax) and section 127.1 (for refundable credits paid in cash to qualifying claimants).

However, any SR&ED ITC claimed or refunded in a taxation year does not constitute a tax-free windfall. Pursuant to paragraph 37(1)(e) and subsection 127.1(3) of the ITA, the amount of federal SR&ED ITC deducted against Part I tax or refunded in cash in a given taxation year is deemed to have been deducted from Part I tax otherwise payable and reduces the balance of the taxpayer's section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures in the immediately following taxation year. If the ITC reduction causes the section 37 pool balance to become negative at the end of that subsequent taxation year, subsection 37(1) and paragraph 12(1)(v) require the negative balance to be included directly in the taxpayer's business income for that subsequent year, effectively taxing the prior year's federal ITC at the taxpayer's prevailing marginal corporate income tax rate in the following year.

body.text: Legislative Evolution and the Enactment of Bill C-15 (March 26, 2026)

Historically, between January 1, 2014 and December 15, 2024, federal SR&ED policy operated under a restrictive posture enacted by the Jobs and Growth Act, 2012, which had reduced the basic ITC rate from 20% to 15%, curtailed the inclusion rate of arm's length contract and third-party payments from 100% to 80%, lowered the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) from 65% to 55%, and completely repealed the eligibility of capital expenditures and capital lease costs under former paragraph 37(1)(b). Over the ensuing decade, two structural deficiencies emerged from this contraction. First, capital-intensive R&D sectors—such as advanced manufacturing, clean technology, semiconductor fabrication, robotics, and biotechnology—were penalized relative to pure software development because physical testbeds, pilot plants, and laboratory instrumentation were excluded from SR&ED support. Second, high-growth Canadian technology companies that completed an initial public offering (IPO) on a domestic stock exchange immediately lost their status as a CCPC, forfeiting the 35% refundable ITC and dropping abruptly to the 15% non-refundable rate.

Following national consultations initiated in Budget 2024 and concrete legislative proposals tabled in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement and Budget 2025 (tabled in Parliament on November 4, 2025), Parliament enacted Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. To operationalize Bill C-15, the CRA released a comprehensive suite of revised statutory forms and administrative policies between April and October 2026, including updated versions of Form T661, Form T1145, and Form T1146 (published May 15, 2026), T2 Schedule 31 (published May 22, 2026), and T2 Schedule 49 (published May 29, 2026), alongside revised editions of the SR&ED Total Qualified Expenditure Policy and SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (May 22, 2026), SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026), SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), and SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (October 7, 2026).
Scientific and Technological Eligibility Criteria and Judicial Precedents
The Four-Part Statutory Definition in Subsection 248(1)

Eligibility for federal and provincial R&D tax incentives in Canada is governed strictly by the definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. Unlike financial accounting definitions of research and development (such as IAS 38 or ASC 730) that encompass commercial product lifecycle engineering, subsection 248(1) establishes a rigorous statutory threshold requiring a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". The statute divides eligible work into three core categories—basic research, applied research, and experimental development—supplemented by a fourth derivative category for directly supporting work.

Under paragraph 248(1)(a), basic research encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view, whereas under paragraph 248(1)(b), applied research encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Paragraph 248(1)(c) codifies experimental development, defined as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto; in practice, the vast majority of industrial SR&ED claims in Canada are filed under this experimental development branch. Complementing these three core pursuits, paragraph 248(1)(d) admits support work with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, provided that such work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer.

Crucially, paragraph 248(1)(d) functions as an exhaustive statutory enumeration of eligible support disciplines. If an activity does not in itself constitute basic research, applied research, or experimental development, it can qualify for SR&ED tax incentives only if it falls within one of those eight enumerated disciplines and is both commensurate with the needs and directly in support of the core SR&ED investigation. Conversely, paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) explicitly exclude seven categories of commercial or routine activity from the definition of SR&ED, even when performed by highly credentialed scientists or engineers: market research or sales promotion (paragraph (e)); quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes (paragraph (f)); research in the social sciences or the humanities (paragraph (g)); prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas (paragraph (h)); the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process (paragraph (i)); style changes (paragraph (j)); and routine data collection (paragraph (k)).
Foundational Jurisprudence: Northwest Hydraulic Consultants and the Five-Question Test

The seminal judicial authority interpreting subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act is the decision of Justice Donald Bowman of the Tax Court of Canada in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 D.T.C. 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520 (TCC). In Northwest Hydraulic, the Tax Court evaluated physical hydraulic modelling projects and articulated a five-criteria legal framework that was subsequently endorsed by the Federal Court of Appeal and incorporated directly into CRA administrative policy as the "Five Questions".

The first judicial criterion asks whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. Justice Bowman emphasized that if the resolution of a technical problem is reasonably predictable using standard procedures known to someone skilled in the art, no technological uncertainty exists. Uncertainty regarding whether a product will be commercially viable, completed within budget, or accepted by the marketplace constitutes business or economic uncertainty rather than technological uncertainty. The second criterion asks whether the person claiming to perform SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty. This requirement entails a five-stage cognitive and experimental methodology comprising the observation of the subject matter of the problem, the formulation of a clear objective, the identification and articulation of the underlying technological uncertainty, the formulation of one or more causal hypotheses designed to reduce or eliminate that uncertainty, and the methodical and systematic testing of the hypotheses by experiment or analysis.

The third criterion examines whether the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses. Intuition, unstructured trial-and-error tinkering, or routine parameter tuning do not satisfy the statutory mandate of a systematic investigation or search. The fourth criterion evaluates whether the process resulted in a technological advancement. A technological advancement represents an advancement in the general understanding of scientific relations or technology known to a person skilled in the relevant field, rather than a mere increase in the internal technical capability of the claimant's own staff through learning publicly available techniques. Importantly, Justice Bowman established that the rejection of a hypothesis is itself a valid technological advancement if it systematically proves that a given technical course of action will not succeed and thereby advances the underlying technological knowledge base. Finally, the fifth criterion asks whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and the results was kept as the work progressed. While appellate jurisprudence has clarified that written documentation is not an independent statutory condition precedent in subsection 248(1), contemporaneous evidence generated as experiments unfold is practically indispensable to discharge the taxpayer's legal burden of proof before a CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) or the Tax Court of Canada.
The CRA's Two-Requirement ("Why" and "How") Administrative Framework

In its consolidated Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives, the CRA streamlined the presentation of the Northwest Hydraulic jurisprudence into a unified Two-Requirement framework—referred to administratively as the "Why" Requirement and the "How" Requirement—while explicitly affirming that both the two requirements and the five questions are derived from the unchanged statutory text of subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act.

body.text: A critical second-order insight for corporate claimants lies in the distinction drawn by the CRA and the Tax Court between technological uncertainty and technical complexity. In complex software architecture, systems integration, or industrial engineering, a project may require thousands of hours of highly skilled labour to integrate third-party application programming interfaces (APIs), migrate legacy databases, or configure cloud microservices. However, if the underlying component behaviours are documented or determinable through vendor specifications and standard engineering patterns, the CRA will classify the effort as routine engineering rather than experimental development. To survive an RTA technical review, the project narrative on Part 2 of Form T661 must isolate the exact boundary where standard practice failed—such as where deterministic algorithms broke down under latency or concurrency constraints, requiring the formulation and experimental validation of novel algorithmic heuristics.
Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Calculation Methodologies, and Pool Mechanics
The Dual-Pool Mechanics: Section 37 vs. Subsection 127(9)

The Canadian SR&ED regime requires claimants to compute two distinct, albeit overlapping, expenditure pools at the conclusion of every taxation year. The first is the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures under subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act, which aggregates the cumulative current and (post-December 15, 2024) capital SR&ED outlays incurred in Canada that may be deducted in computing net income for tax purposes and carried forward indefinitely from year to year. The second is the SR&ED Qualified Expenditure Pool under subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, which defines the annual base of "qualified expenditures" incurred in the taxation year upon which the 15% or 35% SR&ED Investment Tax Credit is calculated. Unlike the section 37 deductible pool, the SR&ED qualified expenditure pool is calculated solely at the end of each specific taxation year and does not carry over to another taxation year; instead, the resulting unused ITCs are eligible for a 3-year carryback and a 20-year carryforward.

Three fundamental structural divergences separate the calculation of the section 37 deductible pool from the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool. First, when a claimant elects the Proxy Method, the notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)—equal to 55% of the eligible SR&ED salary base—is added to the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool to generate ITCs, but is never added to the section 37 deductible expenditure pool because the claimant's actual overhead expenses are already deducted under ordinary business income rules in section 9 of the Act. Second, for arm's length SR&ED contracts and third-party payments, 100% of the eligible current expenditure enters the section 37 deductible expenditure pool, whereas only 80% of the expenditure is included in the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool for ITC purposes. Third, for Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) acquired after December 15, 2024, the partial first-term and second-term amounts enter the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool to earn ITCs, but the capital cost of SUE is excluded from the section 37 deductible expenditure pool and must instead be depreciated under standard Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) rules on Schedule T2SCH8.

body.text: Salaries and Wages and Specified Employee Restrictions

Salaries and wages consistently represent the largest expenditure component of Canadian SR&ED claims. Under paragraph 37(1)(a) and the SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, eligible remuneration encompasses gross salaries, wages, vacation pay, statutory holidays, sick leave, and employer shares of Canada Pension Plan (CPP), Québec Pension Plan (QPP), Employment Insurance (EI), and provincial health or workers' compensation payroll levies paid in respect of employees directly engaged in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Conversely, taxable benefits under sections 6 and 7 of the Income Tax Act (such as employee stock options, automobile standby charges, or taxable group life insurance benefits) and retiring allowances are excluded from SR&ED salaries and wages.

The CRA enforces stringent statutory anti-avoidance limitations for "specified employees"—defined in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act as an employee who is a specified shareholder (owning, directly or indirectly, at any time in the taxation year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the capital stock of the corporation or of any corporation related to it) or who does not deal at arm's length with the corporation, such as a spouse, child, sibling, or parent of a controlling shareholder. For specified employees, four cumulative statutory and administrative restrictions govern claimable remuneration. First, under subsection 37(9), no amount of bonus or remuneration based on profits may be claimed as an SR&ED expenditure for a specified employee. Second, under subsection 37(9.1), the maximum amount of direct SR&ED salary or wages that can be claimed in the section 37 pool and for direct ITC calculation for a specified employee is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan, prorated for the number of days in a short taxation year and shared among associated corporations.

Third, under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations and the SR&ED Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy, the amount of a specified employee's salary that may be included in the salary base to compute the 55% PPA is restricted to the lesser of the actual SR&ED portion of the specified employee's salary, 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages (comprising both SR&ED and non-SR&ED duties, net of bonuses and taxable benefits), and 2.5 times the YMPE, prorated for short taxation years and shared across associated corporations via formal allocation. Fourth, administrative audit guidelines applied by CRA Financial Reviewers generally cap the maximum proportion of a specified employee's time allocable to hands-on SR&ED at 75% to 80%, reflecting the operational reality that owner-managers must devote time to corporate governance, financing, and commercial administration. Additionally, in the context of partnerships, the SR&ED Claims for Partnerships Policy establishes that for income tax purposes, a partner (member) cannot be an employee of the partnership; any salary, wage, or draw paid to a partner is treated by the CRA as a distribution of partnership income rather than a deductible salary expense, and is therefore completely ineligible as an SR&ED salary or wages expenditure.
Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed and Production Runs

Under the Materials for SR&ED Policy, materials claimed for SR&ED must represent tangible property that is either materials consumed or materials transformed directly in the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada. Materials consumed are substances or items that are destroyed or rendered virtually valueless as a result of the SR&ED activity, such as chemical reagents vaporized in a reaction or wood and structural test coupons fractured during destructive testing. General supplies and overhead items do not qualify as materials consumed; the CRA explicitly excludes broken or used laboratory supplies, cleaning supplies, CDs and DVDs, used lubricants such as engine oil, and general utilities such as electricity, natural gas, oil, and general water supply. Only where a specific utility—such as water—is physically consumed directly in the experimental process and the claimant clearly identifies, documents, and allocates that specific portion using a reasonable, supportable, and verifiable methodology can its cost be claimed as a material consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED.

By contrast, materials transformed are tangible materials that are incorporated into another product, prototype, pilot plant, or commercial asset during the course of SR&ED where the resulting property retains some economic value at the conclusion of the experimental work. When experimental development occurs concurrently with manufacturing or industrial production runs, the SR&ED During Production Runs Policy distinguishes between Experimental Development with Experimental Production (ED+EP) and Experimental Development with Commercial Production (ED+CP), establishing that any production run required for SR&ED is treated by default as ED+CP unless it meets the strict definition of ED+EP. If materials transformed during SR&ED are subsequently sold to a customer or converted to commercial use by the claimant, the Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit rules under subsection 127(27) of the Income Tax Act are triggered, requiring the claimant to repay the ITC attributable to the cost of the property or its fair market value or proceeds of disposition.
Overhead Methodologies: Prescribed Proxy Amount (55%) vs. Traditional Method

Every SR&ED claimant must make an annual, irrevocable election on Form T661 for each taxation year to calculate overhead and other expenditures using either the Proxy Method or the Traditional Method. Designed to reduce administrative compliance burdens, the Proxy Method under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations allows the claimant to compute a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) equal to 55% of the eligible SR&ED salary base (direct SR&ED salaries and wages of employees in Canada, subject to the 75% and 2.5× YMPE cap for specified employees). Under the Proxy Method, the claimant does not claim specific overhead costs—such as shop supplies, utilities, office rent, or indirect support staff—on Form T661; instead, those actual expenses are deducted as ordinary business expenses under section 9 of the Income Tax Act, while the notional 55% PPA is added directly to the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool to earn federal and applicable provincial ITCs.

Conversely, when a claimant elects the Traditional Method under subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3) of the Income Tax Regulations, the PPA is nil, and the claimant must identify, track, and substantiate actual overhead and other expenditures incurred in the year under two regulatory branches. The first branch, subsection 2900(2), encompasses expenditures directly attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED, such as incremental travel by SR&ED personnel to test sites, direct clerical or project administration support, and consumable laboratory supplies that do not meet the strict definition of materials consumed. The second branch, subsection 2900(3), encompasses expenditures directly attributable to the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment for the prosecution of SR&ED, such as incremental facility maintenance, specialized utility spikes directly caused by operating an SR&ED test rig, or property insurance attributable to an SR&ED facility. For software, artificial intelligence (AI), FinTech, and biotechnology firms whose primary R&D cost is domestic engineering payroll with minimal physical facility overhead, the Proxy Method (55% PPA) is almost universally superior, as it generates an automatic 1.55× multiplier on eligible non-specified salaries for ITC purposes without requiring invoice-level overhead substantiation during a CRA financial review. The Traditional Method is advantageous primarily for capital- and facility-intensive heavy industrial, mining, or chemical operations where direct SR&ED labour is small relative to massive incremental facility, utility, or post-December 15, 2024 equipment lease outlays.
Cloud Computing, Data Centres, and Software Hosting Costs

A critical area of technical audit friction in the digital economy involves the treatment of cloud computing, Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) cluster rentals, and third-party hosting services used to train large-scale machine learning models or run high-concurrency experimental simulations. Under current CRA statutory interpretation, cloud computing and web-hosting fees do not qualify as "materials consumed or transformed" under paragraph 37(1)(a)(i) of the Income Tax Act because they represent intangible service contracts rather than tangible materials physically destroyed or incorporated into a product. Furthermore, cloud computing fees do not qualify as "contract expenditures for SR&ED performed on behalf of a claimant" under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) because the cloud vendor merely provides compute infrastructure and does not itself perform systematic scientific or technological investigation on the claimant's behalf.

Consequently, if a claimant elects the Proxy Method, third-party cloud computing and web-hosting expenses are treated by the CRA as general overhead captured within the notional 55% PPA allowance and cannot be claimed separately on Form T661. If the claimant elects the Traditional Method, incremental cloud computing costs that are strictly and demonstrably directly attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED (or to the provision of facilities or equipment for SR&ED) may be evaluated under subsections 2900(2) or 2900(3) of the Income Tax Regulations, provided the claimant segregates experimental compute instances completely from commercial production hosting. Recognizing the growing dominance of AI compute expenditures relative to human wages, Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED) and the Department of Finance have prioritized domestic data centre capacity, cloud computing services, and SR&ED modernization across national AI and digital economic strategies.
Subcontractors (SR&ED Contracts) and Third-Party Payments

When a claimant engages external entities to perform R&D, the Contract Expenditures for SR&ED Performed on Behalf of a Claimant Policy and the Third-Party Payments Policy enforce strict statutory distinctions based on whether the performer deals at arm's length with the payer and whether the contract is a direct service contract or a third-party payment.

For arm's length SR&ED contracts governed by subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) and subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, the contracted work must be performed in Canada on behalf of the claimant; current expenditures for SR&ED contract work performed outside Canada are excluded from the section 37 pool and earn no SR&ED ITCs, although they remain deductible as ordinary business expenses in computing net income. Where the work is performed in Canada, 100% of the eligible current contract expenditure enters the payer's section 37 deductible pool, whereas 80% of the expenditure enters the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool for ITC calculation, provided the contract amount is paid or payable to or for the benefit of a "taxable supplier" (generally a Canadian resident person, a Canadian partnership, or a non-resident carrying on business through a Canadian permanent establishment). Under the statutory look-through rule in subsection 37(14), the CRA is empowered to look through an arm's length contract to verify that the contracted SR&ED was physically performed in Canada, that the services were rendered in the claimant's taxation year (subject to the prepaid expense limitation in subsection 18(9)), whether the performer subcontracted the work further, and to reduce the payer's eligible contract expenditure by any capital (non-current) expenditure incurred by the performer where required. Moreover, if an arm's length contractor performs only support work under paragraph 248(1)(d) (such as computer programming, engineering design, or testing) rather than core experimental development, the contract qualifies for the payer only if that support work is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of core SR&ED undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the payer. To prevent duplicate claims on the same underlying research, any payment received by a Canadian contractor from an arm's length taxable supplier for performing SR&ED is defined as a "contract payment" under subsection 127(9), which reduces the contractor's own qualified SR&ED expenditures dollar-for-dollar under subsection 127(18).

Where a claimant (payer) contracts SR&ED work to a related or non-arm's length (NAL) person, the payment is excluded from the payer's qualified expenditures under subsection 127(9). Instead, the NAL performer claims the underlying salaries, materials, and overhead in its own SR&ED pools. If the parties wish for the payer to claim the ITCs, they must execute a joint agreement on Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) under subsections 127(13) to 127(15). The maximum amount transferable on Form T1146 cannot exceed the performer's SR&ED qualified expenditure pool at the end of the taxation year; if the performer attempts to transfer an excess amount, subsection 127(15) renders the excess transfer invalid. Because a partnership is not a "taxpayer" under the Income Tax Act, a partnership cannot transfer or receive qualified SR&ED expenditures under subsection 127(13). Under section 7.4 of the Contract Expenditures Policy, however, where a NAL performer conducts support work under paragraph 248(1)(d) on behalf of a related payer performing core SR&ED, special look-through provisions allow the support work to qualify within the non-arm's length corporate group.

Distinct from direct service contracts, third-party payments under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1) and (ii) are payments made by a claimant to an approved university, college, research institute, or other approved organization (or a non-profit SR&ED corporation) to be used for SR&ED carried on in Canada that is related to a business of the claimant, where the claimant is entitled to exploit the results of the research even though the claimant does not direct or control the day-to-day research execution. Like arm's length contracts, 80% of an eligible third-party payment is included in the claimant's qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes under subsection 127(9), and the claimant must report the project and payment details on Form T661.
Restoration of SR&ED Capital Expenditures and Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

One of the most consequential technical reforms enacted by Bill C-15 (Royal Assent March 26, 2026) is the restoration of SR&ED capital expenditures and equipment lease expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024. Under the updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (published June 29, 2026), SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (published June 8, 2026), and SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (published May 22, 2026), capital outlays made before December 16, 2024 (specifically between January 1, 2014 and December 15, 2024) remain permanently ineligible, whereas depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024 is governed by three distinct statutory tracks.

The first track governs All or Substantially All (ASA) SR&ED Capital Property under paragraph 37(1)(b) and subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act. This regime applies to new or used depreciable property (property eligible for Capital Cost Allowance under paragraph 20(1)(a) owned by the claimant or in which the claimant holds a leasehold interest, excluding property held merely as an agent or nominee) acquired after December 15, 2024. To qualify as ASA property, the claimant must establish at the time of acquisition that the property's anticipated use for non-SR&ED purposes during its operating time over its expected useful life does not exceed 10% (meaning at least 90% of operating time is devoted to SR&ED carried on in Canada), or that not less than 90% of the value of the property is intended to be consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Where a claimant manufactures a capital property in-house for its own SR&ED use, the eligible capital cost includes material, labour, and overhead costs reasonably attributable to the property, excluding any imputed profit that might have been earned had the property been sold. Pursuant to paragraph 2902(b) of the Income Tax Regulations, land (which is a non-depreciable asset) and buildings—including leasehold interests in buildings—are strictly excluded from SR&ED capital expenditures. Qualifying ASA capital expenditures enter the section 37 deductible expenditure pool at 100% (allowing an immediate 100% write-off against taxable income) and enter the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool at 100% to earn the 35% or 15% ITC.

The second track governs Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) under subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act. Where new depreciable machinery and equipment acquired after December 15, 2024 does not meet the 90% ASA threshold, but is used primarily (more than 50% of its operating time) for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, it qualifies under the SUE regime. The capital cost of SUE does not enter the section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures; instead, the claimant must depreciate the capital cost under regular Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) rates and rules on Schedule T2SCH8. However, for ITC purposes under subsection 127(9)—which operates identically under both the Proxy Method and the Traditional Method—SUE generates qualified expenditures across two statutory measurement periods: for "first term shared-use-equipment," 25% of the SR&ED-usage proportion of the capital cost is included in qualified expenditures in the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after acquisition; and for "second term shared-use-equipment," a further 25% of the SR&ED-usage proportion is included in qualified expenditures in the subsequent taxation year ending at least 24 months after acquisition, yielding a cumulative 50% qualified expenditure inclusion on the SR&ED-usage proportion.

The third track governs Equipment Lease Expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024. While lease costs incurred before December 16, 2024 (from January 1, 2014 to December 15, 2024) do not qualify for SR&ED tax incentives, lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 for equipment used ASA (at least 90% of operating time after December 15, 2024) or as SUE (more than 50% of operating time) qualify under the updated SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy.
Unpaid Amounts (Subsection 127(26)) and ITC Recapture (Subsections 127(27)–(34))

Two statutory clawback mechanisms require vigilant tracking by tax auditors and corporate controllers: the 180-day unpaid amounts rule and the ITC recapture regime. Under subsection 127(26) of the Income Tax Act, if an otherwise eligible SR&ED expenditure—such as an accrued bonus for a non-specified employee, an unpaid invoice to an arm's length SR&ED subcontractor, or an accrued material cost—is incurred in a taxation year but remains unpaid on the day that is 180 days after the end of the taxation year, the unpaid amount is deemed not to have been incurred in that taxation year for the purpose of calculating the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool. Instead, the expenditure is deemed to be incurred—and earns ITCs—only in the subsequent taxation year in which it is actually paid.

Complementing the unpaid amounts rule, the Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit rules under subsections 127(27) to 127(34) of the Income Tax Act and the Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy apply whenever a claimant acquires or produces a property whose cost was included in qualified SR&ED expenditures—including materials transformed into a custom product, commercial asset, or experimental production run; ASA capital equipment; Shared-Use Equipment; animals or other growing things used in SR&ED projects; or tangible property acquired through an SR&ED contract—and subsequently disposes of the property or converts it to commercial use. When recapture is triggered, the recaptured amount is added directly to the claimant's Part I federal tax payable for the taxation year of disposition or conversion (and increases the section 37 deductible pool by the corresponding amount), equal to the lesser of the actual SR&ED ITC originally earned in respect of the particular property, and the amount determined by multiplying the historical ITC rate percentage used when the property was claimed by either the proceeds of disposition (if sold to an arm's length party) or the fair market value of the property at the time of disposition or conversion (if sold to a non-arm's length party or converted to commercial use).

Two specialized audit distinctions govern ITC recapture under subsections 127(27) and 127(32). First, recapture applies exclusively to tangible property, not intellectual property (IP). If a payer contracts SR&ED to a performer where IP rights vest in the payer under the terms of the original contract, the IP accrued to the payer as it was generated and the payer will not face ITC recapture if it subsequently sells or licenses the IP. Similarly, if the IP rights vest in the performer under the SR&ED contract and the payer subsequently pays a separate lump sum under a second contract to acquire the IP rights from the performer, the payment to acquire IP rights is not an allowable SR&ED expenditure under section 37, and the performer is not required to recapture its ITC on the sale of the IP. Second, section 7.1 of the Recapture Policy highlights a significant structural disparity between outsourced and in-house component fabrication under subsection 127(32): if a corporation orders a custom SR&ED part from an arm's length supplier for $12,000 (comprising a $10,000 manufacturing and development cost plus a $2,000 profit element), the cost of the property subject to recapture upon commercial conversion is the full $12,000. Conversely, if that exact same part is manufactured in-house by the claimant, only the raw material cost is subject to recapture; there is no recapture on the in-house SR&ED salaries or overhead costs incurred to fabricate the component.
Federal Investment Tax Credit (ITC) Rates, Thresholds, Refundability, and Carryforwards
The Enhanced 35% Rate vs. the Basic 15% Rate

The federal SR&ED program operates a two-tier ITC rate structure under subsections 127(9) and 127(10.1) of the Income Tax Act. The Enhanced 35% ITC Rate applies to qualified SR&ED expenditures up to the claimant's annual expenditure limit. For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, this enhanced 35% rate was restricted exclusively to Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) on up to $3,000,000 of annual qualified expenditures, generating a maximum annual credit of $1,050,000 at the 35% rate. Under Bill C-15, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, eligibility for the 35% enhanced rate is expanded to both CCPCs and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and the maximum annual expenditure limit is doubled to $6,000,000, yielding up to $2,100,000 per year in 35% refundable ITCs. Conversely, the Basic 15% ITC Rate applies to all qualified SR&ED expenditures that do not qualify for the 35% enhanced rate—including expenditures incurred by foreign-controlled corporations, large public or private corporations whose expenditure limit has phased out to nil, partnerships (allocated to active members under subsection 127(8)), individuals (sole proprietors), and trusts, as well as CCPC or ECPC qualified expenditures that exceed the corporation's annual expenditure limit.
Mathematical Formulation of the Expenditure Limit Phase-Out (Post-December 15, 2024)

Under subsections 127(10.2) and 127(10.6) of the Income Tax Act as amended by Bill C-15, the $6,000,000 annual expenditure limit for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 is subject to a linear phase-out based on corporate size, with two distinct statutory measurement methodologies depending on whether the claimant is a CCPC using the taxable capital test or an ECPC (or an electing CCPC) using the consolidated revenue test.
1. The Taxable Capital Phase-Out Formula for CCPCs

For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, a CCPC's $3,000,000 expenditure limit began decreasing once its prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada (computed across the CCPC and all associated corporations) reached $10,000,000, and was completely eliminated at $50,000,000. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 expanded the base limit to $6,000,000 and widened the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range to $15,000,000 to $75,000,000. Let TC denote the aggregate taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC and its associated corporations for the immediately preceding taxation year (in dollars), and let D denote the number of days in the taxation year. 2. The Average Annual Revenue Phase-Out Method for ECPCs and Electing CCPCs

Because public corporations are not subject to the CCPC small business deduction capital structure in the same manner as private firms, Bill C-15 introduced the Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) category for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. To determine the expenditure limit for an ECPC—or for a CCPC that formally elects to use the ECPC method for a taxation year beginning after December 15, 2024—the Income Tax Act requires computing the average annual revenue reflected in the financial statements over the 3 preceding fiscal years for the corporation and every corporation that is a member of its group in the taxation year, regardless of whether the corporations were associated throughout the entirety of that three-year period. The statute permits reasonable adjustments—such as eliminating intra-group sales of goods or services—so that the annual revenue of the group accurately reflects that of a single economic entity.
Associated Corporations, Short Tax Years, and Anti-Avoidance Rules

Where two or more CCPCs are associated with each other in a taxation year under section 256 of the Income Tax Act, they must share a single $6,000,000 expenditure limit (as reduced by their combined prior-year taxable capital) by filing T2 Schedule 49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit). Similarly, ECPCs that are members of a consolidated group must share the expenditure limit across the group.

The SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy enforces specific statutory rules where a CCPC or ECPC has more than one taxation year ending in the same calendar year (for example, due to a change in fiscal year-end) and is associated in two or more of those taxation years with another CCPC (or is a member of a consolidated group with another ECPC) that has a taxation year ending in that same calendar year. In such cases, the corporation's expenditure limit for the second (short) taxation year ending in that calendar year must match the allocation made for its first taxation year ending in that calendar year, prorated strictly by the number of days in the short taxation year divided by 365 (for instance, an allocated $3,000,000 share of the limit prorated over a 6-month period from July 1 to December 31 yields an expenditure limit of $1,512,328). Furthermore, under the SR&ED anti-avoidance provisions, two or more corporations are deemed to be associated with each other if one of the main reasons for the separate existence of those corporations is to reduce the amount of income tax otherwise payable or to increase the amount of refundable SR&ED ITCs available, unless specific shareholder relief conditions are satisfied.
Refundability Mechanics, Partnerships, and Loss Restriction Events

The cash refundability of federal SR&ED ITCs under section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act depends on the taxpayer's legal classification, the ITC rate earned, and whether the expenditure falls within or above the annual expenditure limit. Any ITC that is not refunded in cash may be applied to reduce Part I federal income tax otherwise payable in the current taxation year, carried back up to 3 taxation years, or carried forward up to 20 taxation years.

body.text: Two specialized structural regimes govern partnerships and corporate acquisitions of control (loss restriction events). Because a partnership is a flow-through arrangement rather than a distinct taxpayer, a partnership cannot carry forward a section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures to future years; the entire section 37 pool at the end of the partnership's fiscal period must be fully deducted in calculating the partnership's net income or loss for tax purposes in that year. Moreover, if a deduction for SR&ED expenditures creates or increases a partnership net loss, the amount of that partnership loss attributable to SR&ED is disallowed to a limited partner, is not allowed to other partners, and does not become a limited partnership loss or a non-capital loss. Similarly, under subsection 127(8) of the Income Tax Act, SR&ED ITCs computed at the partnership level (at the 15% rate) cannot be allocated to a "specified member" of the partnership—defined as any limited partner or any passive general partner who was not regularly, continuously, and substantially actively engaged in the activities of the partnership's business (other than financing) or carrying on a similar business during the partnership's fiscal period. However, SR&ED ITCs barred from allocation to specified members do not vanish; they remain available to be allocated in full to the active general partners (non-specified members) of the partnership.

When a corporation or trust undergoes a "loss restriction event" (such as an acquisition of control by an unrelated purchaser), both its undeducted section 37 SR&ED expenditure pool and its unused 20-year ITC carryforwards or post-acquisition carrybacks are restricted. Specifically, under section 8.0 of the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures Policy, pre-acquisition section 37 pool balances can be deducted in subsequent taxation years only when the business to which the SR&ED expenditure related continues to be carried on for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit, and only to the extent that the corporation's income for the taxation year (before making any deduction from the section 37 pool) is derived from that same business or a similar business. Analogous streaming restrictions limit the carryforward and carryback of unused ITCs following an acquisition of control.
Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes and Federal-Provincial Stacking

Every Canadian province (except Prince Edward Island, which delivers R&D support through direct grants and rebates rather than corporate tax statute credits) and the Yukon Territory provide statutory corporate income tax incentives for R&D conducted within their territorial boundaries. With the exception of Québec and Alberta, all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits are administered by the CRA under federal-provincial tax collection agreements, adopt the federal definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, and require the claimant to file a valid federal Form T661.

1. Ontario (OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC)

Ontario operates a multi-layered R&D incentive architecture that allows qualifying corporations with an Ontario permanent establishment to stack up to three distinct tax credits on the same project portfolio. First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC), claimed on Schedule 566, provides an 8% refundable tax credit (10% for taxation years ending before June 1, 2016) on up to $3,000,000 of qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures, yielding a maximum annual cash refund of $240,000. The $3,000,000 OITC expenditure limit must be shared among associated corporations, is prorated for short taxation years based on the number of days in proportion to 365, and is gradually reduced if the corporation's prior-year federal taxable income lies between $500,000 and $800,000 or if its prior-year taxable capital lies between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000. Importantly, in parallel with recent federal enhancements under Bill C-15, Ontario updated both the OITC and the ORDTC so that qualified expenditures include 100% of current expenditures and 100% of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024 (while continuing to exclude capital expenditures made after December 31, 2013 and before December 16, 2024).

Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC), claimed on Schedule 508, provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit (4.5% prior to June 1, 2016) available to all corporations with an Ontario permanent establishment regardless of size. Because the OITC is treated as government assistance that reduces eligible expenditures for the ORDTC, a small business claiming both credits must reduce its ORDTC eligible expenditure base by the 8% OITC earned, yielding an effective combined Ontario credit on the first $3,000,000 of expenditures of 11.22% (8% + 3.5% × 92%). Any unused portion of the ORDTC may be carried back 3 years and carried forward 20 years to reduce Ontario corporate income tax payable, and if property included in a previous ORDTC claim is subsequently disposed of or converted to commercial use, Ontario recapture rules apply using a statutory 23.56% calculation rate. Third, where an Ontario corporation incurs qualified expenditures under an eligible contract with a qualifying Ontario university, college, or research institute, it may claim the 20% fully refundable Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC) on Schedule 568, subject to a $20,000,000 annual expenditure cap.
2. Québec (Autonomous Administration by Revenu Québec)

Québec is the only jurisdiction in Canada that administers its personal, trust, partnership, and corporate income tax regime—including R&D tax incentives—autonomously through Revenu Québec. Claimants conducting R&D in Québec claim the flagship Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) on Form RD-1029.7-V. The base rate of the Québec Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) is 14% (fully refundable), which is also the standard rate applicable to members of a partnership filing Form RD-1029.7-V. For qualifying SMEs, the refundable tax credit rate rises up to 30% on eligible R&D salaries, phasing down based on the corporation's prior-year assets (where a corporation may elect under specific rules to compute assets net of liabilities). Furthermore, Revenu Québec applies an exclusion threshold (seuil d'exclusion) to qualified R&D expenditures before computing the credit, including a $12,500 exclusion threshold amount related to a qualified property in partnership allocations. In its budget of March 25, 2025, the Québec government announced the replacement of the Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) and other R&D tax credits by a new refundable tax credit for R&D, innovation and pre-commercialization (crédit d'impôt pour la R-D, l'innovation et la précommercialisation, CRIC) for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, at a rate of 20% on eligible expenditures exceeding the exclusion threshold, rising to 30% on up to $1,000,000 of those expenditures.
3. British Columbia (Full Harmonization with Bill C-15 via BC Bill 2, 2026)

Governed by Part 6 (section 97) of the Income Tax Act (British Columbia) and updated by Bill 2, Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026, the British Columbia SR&ED Tax Credit—claimed on Form T666 and reported on lines 659 and 674 of T2 Schedule 5—was fully harmonized in 2026 with the federal Bill C-15 expansions. Qualifying corporations that are either CCPCs or Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) with a permanent establishment in British Columbia may claim a 10% fully refundable tax credit on the lesser of their SR&ED qualified BC expenditure for the taxation year and their federal expenditure limit as determined under subsections 127(10.2) and 127(10.6) of the federal Income Tax Act. Effective for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, British Columbia doubled its refundable expenditure limit from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 (yielding up to $600,000 in refundable BC credits per year), increased the prior-year taxable capital phase-out threshold range to $15,000,000 to $75,000,000, and restored the eligibility of capital expenditures as BC qualified expenditures.

All qualifying corporations (including CCPC and ECPC expenditures exceeding the refundable expenditure limit, as well as active corporate members of a partnership) may claim a 10% non-refundable BC SR&ED tax credit on their remaining qualified BC expenditures less any refundable credit claimed and any amount formally renounced for that year. Unused non-refundable BC credits can be carried back 3 years and forward 10 years, and if property on which a BC SR&ED credit was claimed is disposed of or converted to commercial use within 10 years of acquisition, BC recapture rules apply to increase BC tax payable or reduce the tax refund. Claimants must submit Form T666 to the CRA no later than 18 months after the end of the taxation year in which the qualified expenditures are incurred; individuals are not eligible for the BC SR&ED tax credit.
4. Alberta (The Innovation Employment Grant – IEG)

Enacted under Bill 35, Tax Statutes (Creating Jobs and Driving Innovation) Amendment Act, 2020 (Royal Assent December 9, 2020), which added Division 7 to Part 6 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act effective January 1, 2021, the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) is delivered through the Alberta corporate tax system via AT1 Schedule 29 without requiring a separate pre-application. Eligible expenditures must be incurred in Alberta after December 31, 2020 and match those that qualify for the federal SR&ED program. The IEG provides qualified corporations with an 8% base payment for eligible R&D spending carried out in Alberta up to the corporation's base level of spending (calculated as the corporation's average qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the preceding 2 taxation years), plus an enhanced 20% payment on eligible Alberta R&D spending that exceeds that two-year base spending level, up to a maximum cap of $4,000,000 in annual R&D spending. To focus support on small and medium-sized enterprises, the grant phases out incrementally for corporations with between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 in taxable capital, and firms with $50,000,000 or more in taxable capital are ineligible.
Federal-Provincial Assistance Grinding and Strategic Renunciation

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18) of the federal Income Tax Act, all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits (including Alberta's IEG) constitute "government assistance" in respect of SR&ED. Consequently, any provincial R&D credit that a claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing due date for the taxation year reduces the federal qualified SR&ED expenditure pool dollar-for-dollar before the 35% or 15% federal ITC is computed.

A nuanced statutory interaction occurs when a claimant uses the Proxy Method in a province whose R&D tax credit base includes the federal Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA). Under section 4.5.2 of the CRA Assistance and Contract Payments Policy and subsection 127(18) of the Income Tax Act, the entire provincial or territorial R&D tax credit—including the portion that relates to the notional 55% PPA—reduces the federal qualified SR&ED expenditure pool for ITC purposes, regardless of whether the provincial credit is refundable or non-refundable. However, under section 4.5.1 of the Assistance Policy and paragraph 37(1)(d) of the Income Tax Act, because the notional PPA is not an actual expenditure included in the section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures, the portion of the provincial or territorial R&D tax credit attributable to the PPA is not applied to reduce the section 37 deductible pool; instead, under the Proxy Method, that PPA-related portion of the provincial credit must be included directly in the taxpayer's income under paragraph 12(1)(x) of the Income Tax Act in the taxation year in which it is received.

Furthermore, if a corporation is in a tax-loss position and earns a non-refundable provincial R&D credit (such as the 3.5% Ontario ORDTC, the 10% non-refundable BC SR&ED credit, or the non-refundable Saskatchewan R&D credit) that it cannot utilize against provincial tax payable in the near term, that unutilized provincial credit would still immediately grind down its current-year federal qualified SR&ED expenditure pool and federal cash refund. To avoid sacrificing immediate federal cash ITCs for an unusable provincial carryforward, provincial statutes (including British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia, and Ontario) permit a corporation to formally renounce its entitlement to all or part of the provincial R&D tax credit on or before the income tax return filing due date (6 months after the corporation's tax year-end). In circumstances where the claimant validly renounces the provincial R&D tax credit by the filing due date of the income tax return, neither the federal section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures nor the subsection 127(9) qualified SR&ED expenditures are reduced by the renounced credit.
Interaction with Direct Government Grants and Non-Dilutive Funding ("Stacking")

Canadian R&D performers frequently combine retroactive SR&ED tax credits with prospective, application-based government grants—such as the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) and Alberta Innovates voucher and TIER programs. While direct government grants and non-government assistance reduce both the section 37 pool under paragraph 37(1)(d) and the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool under subsection 127(18), the structure of the Proxy Method creates a highly advantageous mathematical "shielding" effect for salary-based grants like NRC IRAP.
The Proxy Method Stacking Advantage with NRC IRAP

NRC IRAP typically reimburses a specified percentage of direct internal technical salaries and wages, but does not reimburse corporate overhead. Under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations and the SR&ED Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy, a claimant's 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is calculated on the gross eligible SR&ED salary base before deducting government assistance. The government assistance (such as the NRC IRAP grant) is then subtracted only at the subsequent stage when computing net qualified SR&ED expenditures under subsection 127(18) on Form T661.

To illustrate this second-order structural benefit, consider a qualifying CCPC in Ontario (eligible for the 35% federal ITC, 8% Ontario OITC, and 3.5% Ontario ORDTC) that incurs $1,000,000 in direct non-specified SR&ED salaries and wages in a taxation year beginning after December 15, 2024, and elects the Proxy Method (55% PPA), comparing a scenario with no grant against a scenario where the CCPC receives a $500,000 NRC IRAP grant (50% salary reimbursement).

Conversely, where each member of a non-arm's length group performs SR&ED and the assistance received is less than the total qualified SR&ED expenditures of the group on the project, the parties may allocate the assistance among the group members using prescribed Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length), filed by the transferor's filing due date for the taxation year or within the period in which the transferor may serve a Notice of Objection for the year. Administrative Governance, Filing Procedures, Audit Protocols, and Judicial Appeals
Prescribed Forms, Mandatory Information, and the Strict 18-Month Statutory Deadline

Access to both the section 37 expenditure deduction and the section 127 Investment Tax Credit is conditioned upon strict compliance with the statutory filing requirements set forth in subsections 37(11) and 127(9)(m) of the Income Tax Act and the SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy. To deduct an allowable SR&ED expenditure or earn an SR&ED ITC, a claimant must file the prescribed forms containing the prescribed information on or before the day that is 12 months after the claimant's income tax return filing due date for the taxation year. Because a corporation's T2 income tax return filing due date is 6 months after the end of its taxation year, the SR&ED reporting deadline for a corporation is 18 months after the end of the taxation year. Where the claimant is a partnership, the partnership filing rules in section 6.4 of the Filing Requirements Policy and the SR&ED Claims for Partnerships Policy govern: if the members of the partnership are a combination of individuals (including trusts) and corporations, the partnership information return due date is no later than the earlier of March 31 after the calendar year in which the fiscal period ended or the day that is 5 months after the end of the partnership's fiscal period, from which the 12-month SR&ED reporting window is measured.

The 18-month corporate filing deadline applies equally to any original or amended prescribed form for SR&ED and operates as an absolute statutory bar. If a claimant fails to file the prescribed forms containing the prescribed information within the 12-month window following the tax return filing due date, the expenditures are statutorily deemed not to be SR&ED expenditures and no ITC is earned on those outlays. To reflect the legislative reforms of Bill C-15, the CRA published an updated suite of prescribed SR&ED forms in May 2026: Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim, published May 15, 2026), which includes the Field of Research (FOR) code used by Statistics Canada to collect data on Canadian R&D; Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, published May 15, 2026); Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, published May 15, 2026); T2 Schedule 31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations, published May 22, 2026); and T2 Schedule 49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit, published May 29, 2026).
The New Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026) and Portal Upgrades

Historically, the retroactive nature of SR&ED reviews meant that businesses incurred R&D expenditures throughout their fiscal year, filed Form T661 up to 18 months later, and only learned whether the CRA accepted their technical eligibility after a post-filing review. To eliminate this lag and improve predictability, the CRA officially launched the optional Pre-Claim Approval Process on April 1, 2026, alongside digital upgrades to the SR&ED Client Portal (accessed via My Business Account) and the Self-Assessment and Learning Tool (SALT).

Through a streamlined application submitted in My Business Account, eligible businesses can obtain a formal Pre-Claim Approval determination from the CRA within eight weeks, allowing them to ascertain whether their planned R&D projects qualify for SR&ED tax incentives before starting work or incurring any costs. To support prospective claimants, the CRA also offers one-on-one pre-claim approval sessions, financial deep dives, and guided workshops upon request via OESCPB-SVEDGPO@cra-arc.gc.ca, while the upgraded SR&ED Client Portal provides a pre-claim workbook to compile Form T661 information, an exclusive save-and-retrieve version of the Self-Assessment and Learning Tool, direct options to request assistance from an SR&ED specialist, and up-front processing time information. Furthermore, the CRA updated The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants in 2026 to establish clear protocols for claims selected for post-filing review after receiving pre-claim approval, supporting the federal government's Budget 2025 commitment to cut the overall processing period for SR&ED claims in half.
CRA Dual-Track Review and Audit Protocols

When a filed SR&ED claim is selected for examination, the CRA conducts a coordinated review governed by The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants and the Program Financial Claim Review Manual (Review Procedures for Financial Reviewers). During this process, a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) evaluates whether the claimed work meets the statutory definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act (applying the "Why" and "How" requirements), while a Financial Reviewer (FR) verifies the eligibility and calculation of claimed expenditures, assistance, unpaid amounts, and provincial schedules.

At the conclusion of the examination, where adjustments are proposed, the CRA issues a Proposal Letter accompanied by a Summary of Adjustments. The Financial Reviewer's report must document whether the claimant agrees with the proposed adjustments (confirmed by signing and dating the Summary of Adjustments or submitting a confirmation letter), disagrees with some or all of the proposed adjustments, has made representations where concurrence remains unclear, or has not responded orally or in writing. Under section 6.4.5 of the Financial Claim Review Manual, a documentation package for CRA Headquarters is required for any changed file where the permanent income change exceeds ±$2,000,000, the permanent tax change exceeds ±$400,000, the net present value of the tax earned by audit (TEBA-NPV) exceeds ±$400,000, or the net present value of the tax protected changes (TPRO-NPV) exceeds ±$1,000,000. In addition, the Minister may grant relief from penalties and/or interest where extraordinary circumstances (such as flood, fire, or illness), actions of the CRA (such as undue delays in completing a review), or inability to pay or financial hardship exist. Once the review is finalized, a Notice of Assessment or Notice of Reassessment is issued, advising the claimant of its right to object within 90 days.
Administrative Objections and Judicial Appeals to the Tax Court of Canada

When a taxpayer disagrees with a Notice of Assessment or Notice of Reassessment disallowing or reducing an SR&ED claim, the statutory dispute resolution architecture under Part I, Division J of the Income Tax Act (sections 165 to 171) governs administrative objections and judicial appeals.

body.text: A critical statutory restriction governs income tax objections and appeals filed by "large corporations" under subsections 165(1.11) and 165(1.13) of the Income Tax Act. In addition to standard objection details, subsection 165(1.11) requires a large corporation to specify in its Notice of Objection a description of each issue, the exact amount of relief sought in respect of each issue, and the facts and reasons relied on by the corporation. Pursuant to subsection 165(1.13), a large corporation is statutorily prohibited from raising new issues or revising the amount of relief sought with respect to an issue in an objection to an assessment made under the provisions or circumstances referred to in paragraph 165(1.1)(a). Furthermore, subsection 165(1.2) restricts any taxpayer from objecting to the assessment of an issue where the taxpayer has waived the right of objection in writing. Consequently, following the Bill C-15 expansion of the 35% enhanced ITC phase-out ceiling to $75,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital, mid-market corporations whose taxable capital exceeds the $10,000,000 large-corporation threshold must ensure that any Notice of Objection under subsection 165(1) strictly satisfies the issue-by-issue quantum pleading mandates of subsection 165(1.11).
Strategic Conclusions and Compliance Recommendations for Canadian R&D Claimants

The enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026 marks a watershed structural expansion of Canada's R&D tax architecture, reversing over a decade of statutory contraction and repositioning the federal SR&ED program—alongside harmonized provincial regimes in British Columbia and Ontario—as a premier global vehicle for industrial innovation. Analysis of the post-Bill C-15 statutory framework yields five core strategic imperatives for corporate claimants, tax counsel, and R&D auditors.

First, capital-intensive R&D performers in clean technology, advanced manufacturing, life sciences, and hardware engineering should immediately re-architect their capital budgeting and fixed-asset registers for depreciable property and equipment leases incurred after December 15, 2024. By segregating post-December 15, 2024 R&D equipment acquisitions into All or Substantially All (at least 90% of operating time) and Shared-Use Equipment (more than 50% of operating time) classifications, and leveraging the parallel restoration of capital expenditure eligibility under Ontario's OITC and ORDTC as well as British Columbia's SR&ED tax credit, qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs can recover up to 41.22% to 45% of eligible capital outlays in combined federal and provincial tax credits while deducting 100% of ASA capital costs in the section 37 pool in the year of acquisition.

Second, publicly traded Canadian technology, biotechnology, and industrial innovation companies should audit their corporate structure and three-year consolidated financial statements to qualify as Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. Under Bill C-15 and British Columbia's Bill 2 (2026), qualifying ECPCs are no longer penalized for listing on a public stock exchange and can access up to $2,100,000 annually in 35% refundable federal SR&ED ITCs alongside up to $600,000 annually in 10% refundable British Columbia SR&ED tax credits on up to $6,000,000 of qualified expenditures.

Third, venture-backed or asset-heavy CCPCs whose prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,000—which would otherwise begin grinding down their $6,000,000 expenditure limit across the $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 phase-out range—should model the statutory election introduced for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 that allows a CCPC to compute its expenditure limit using the ECPC three-year average annual revenue method. For pre-revenue or early-commercialisation CCPCs carrying high paid-up capital or debt from financing rounds, electing the three-year revenue method can preserve the full $6,000,000 enhanced expenditure limit.

Fourth, claimants planning multi-year R&D initiatives or projects near the boundary of standard engineering practice should proactively utilize the CRA's Pre-Claim Approval Process launched on April 1, 2026 via the My Business Account SR&ED Client Portal. Securing an up-front eligibility determination within the CRA's eight-week service window before commencing work or incurring costs de-risks R&D capital allocation and accelerates post-filing refund issuance.

Finally, notwithstanding the administrative modernization of the SR&ED Client Portal and Pre-Claim Approval Process, the legal burden of proof under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act and the Northwest Hydraulic doctrine remains anchored in contemporaneous experimental evidence. Claimants must embed systematic hypothesis-and-test tracking into their daily engineering workflows, monitor the 180-day unpaid amount deadline under subsection 127(26), execute timely non-arm's length transfers and assistance allocations on updated Forms T1145 and T1146, and—where taxable capital exceeds $10,000,000—ensure strict compliance with the large-corporation objection pleading rules of subsection 165(1.11).
